title: Why does the first price matter?
principle: The first number buyers see sets what every price feels like.

screens.text: Let me tell you about an odd test from the 1970s. Two scientists, Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman, spun a wheel with numbers in front of people. The wheel could stop only at 10 or 65. Then they asked about Africa.

screens.title: A question about Africa
screens.text: They asked two things. First: is the percent of UN countries in Africa higher or lower than the wheel's number? (The UN is a group of countries from around the world.) Then: what percent do you guess? The wheel had nothing to do with Africa.

screens.prompt: Some people saw the wheel stop at 65, others at 10. Then they guessed what percent of UN countries are in Africa. What happened?

options.label: Both groups guessed about the same

screens.why: The typical guess was 45% for those who saw 65, and 25% for those who saw 10. The wheel's number moved their guesses from 25% to 45%.

screens.title: Anchoring
screens.text: Scientists call this anchoring. A ship's anchor stops it from moving far. The first number you see does the same to your thinking. You guess above or below it, but stay too close. This happens even when you know the number means nothing.

screens.title: It's used on you
screens.text: You'll see this in shops. A sale page says "MRP ₹2,999, now ₹1,199". The old price has a line through it. That number is the anchor: it makes ₹1,199 seem cheap. When you bargain, the first fair-sounding price is the anchor. Did anyone really pay ₹2,999? Often, nobody did.

screens.prompt: A website shows a shirt: "Was ₹2,999, now ₹1,199". Nobody ever paid ₹2,999. What is the ₹2,999 doing?

options.label: Showing what the shirt is really worth
Showing what the shop paid for the shirt
A false price to make you buy

screens.why: Yes. Nobody paid ₹2,999, so it's not the shirt's real value. It's shown only to make ₹1,199 feel cheap.

wrong.a: Nobody ever paid ₹2,999, so it's not the shirt's real value. It's a fake anchor to make ₹1,199 feel cheap.
wrong.b: Shops don't show what they paid on a sale page. Nobody paid ₹2,999. It's a fake anchor to make ₹1,199 feel cheap.

screens.title: Now look at your business
screens.text: A test with a wheel can teach you about your home bakery. It's January of your fourth year. Your chocolate birthday cake now sells for ₹850, and you keep ₹450 from each one. You also make a big two-tier party cake for ₹2,500.

screens.prompt: Your WhatsApp menu shows a ₹850 cake and a ₹2,500 party cake. Some families say ₹850 is "too costly". Which should you show first?

options.label: The ₹850 cake, so families don't get scared
The ₹2,500 party cake, then the ₹850 cake
Neither: hide prices until they ask

screens.why: Yes. You do sell the ₹2,500 cake. Show it first, so ₹850 feels fair. When a buyer says "too costly", ask: compared to which price? Then change what they compare it with.

wrong.a: Then ₹850 is the first price they see, so it feels high. Show your real ₹2,500 party cake first. After that, ₹850 feels fair.
wrong.c: Then they ask, and ₹850 is still the first price they hear. Show your real ₹2,500 party cake first. After that, ₹850 feels fair.

screens.prompt: I'll show you six anchors. For each one, tell me: is it honest, or a trick?

items.text: Show your real ₹2,500 party cake first
Tell buyers the big chain shop's cake costs ₹1,100, which is true
Write "MRP ₹1,500" on a cake you always sell at ₹850
For a big order, start with a price you can explain
Ask ₹5,000 for an ₹850 cake, hoping to come down to ₹1,500

screens.why: Honest anchors use real prices: a cake you sell, a price another shop charges, or a price you can explain. Tricks use fake prices or numbers you can't explain.

screens.setup: It's late January. An office wants 30 boxes of cupcakes for a staff party. Each box costs you ₹150 to make. Big shops charge about ₹400 a box. The manager knows this. She asks, "What's your price?"
screens.question: What do you say first?

options.label: ₹600 a box, so you can bargain down
options.outcome: The manager looks unhappy: "Big shops charge ₹400." She doesn't ask for a lower price. She thanks you and calls another baker. You lose the order.
options.why: You can start with a high price only if you can explain it. ₹600 looked like a trick when big shops charged ₹400.
options.better: ₹350 a box, and show that big shops charge ₹400.

options.label: ₹350 a box, next to the ₹400 shops
options.outcome: You say: "₹350 a box, fresh from my kitchen. Big shops charge about ₹400." She asks for ₹320. You agree on ₹330. Each of the 30 boxes leaves you ₹180: ₹5,400.
options.why: You started with a price you could explain and compared it with a real price. That first price led to a fair deal.

options.label: ₹250 a box, so she won't buy elsewhere
options.outcome: She says yes at once, too fast. 30 boxes leave ₹100 each: ₹3,000. Later, she says she had planned to pay ₹350 a box.
options.why: You got the order, but your low first price decided the deal. You can't raise it after saying it.
options.better: ₹350 a box, and show that big shops charge ₹400.

screens.title: The honest line
screens.text: Here's the rule for this whole module: use on others only what you'd accept being used on you. In simple words: treat buyers as you'd want a shop to treat you. Showing a real cake first is fair. Showing a fake "was" price is not.
The ___ number a buyer sees changes how every ___ feels.
screens.why: Exactly. The wheel moved people's guesses from 25% to 45%. Show your real ₹2,500 party cake first, and ₹850 feels fair.

summary: Anchoring: the first number you see affects your thinking, even when it means nothing.
Crossed-out MRPs and "was" prices are anchors. Ask: did anyone ever pay that price?
Show a real, higher-priced option first. Start a deal with a price you can explain. Never use a fake "was" price.

cards.front: A phone website says "MRP ₹40,000, now ₹24,999". The phone never sold at ₹40,000. What is ₹40,000?
cards.back: A price nobody paid is an anchor. It makes the price you pay feel cheap.

cards.front: You sell a ₹600 thali and a ₹250 one. Which should a new customer see first on the menu?
cards.back: Show a real, higher-priced option first. It makes the other prices feel fair.

cards.front: A shop asks your price for a big order. Nearby shops charge ₹400. What price should you say first?
cards.back: The first price helps decide the deal. Start with a price you can explain.

sources.label: Tversky and Kahneman, Judgment under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases (Science, 1974)
